A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 28 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original bias-detection experiments, simulated labeling-strategy updates, runtime measurements, ablations, and a human-versus-LLM sycophancy-rating pilot.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds reward-model retraining experiments, validation-distribution testing, and human audits of original preference labels.

M1.justification: The DataInf/OPORP estimator, reward-model architecture and objective, and SVM strategy update are retained. Appendix G adds a limited extension that directly flips the highest-influence preference labels and retrains the reward model, turning detection into dataset correction.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation from synthetically injected biases to naturally occurring annotation errors in unmodified Anthropic-HH. It also tests Anthropic-HH bias detection using a HelpSteer2 validation set. These introduce substantive natural-error and distribution-mismatch scenarios despite retaining the same dataset families.

E2.justification: The original named detector and DataInf comparisons remain. v2 adds random selection against influence-ranked selection in the human surveys and clean-data reward models as retraining controls. Appendix C.2.3 also corrects the published confidence and entropy score signs; rerunning the retained comparisons is not established.

E3.justification: New protocols include retraining after correcting 50%, 100%, or 150% of the injected corruption count; constructing 145 HelpSteer2 validation pairs using helpfulness and response length; and auditing 100 selected versus 100 random samples per bias with four annotators, anonymized response pairs, and ties allowed. The original main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds an intervention study testing whether influence-guided label correction improves reward models, including correction-rate sensitivity and opposing validation subsets. Appendix I.4 adds validation-distribution robustness testing, and Appendix J adds original-label error analyses and examples. Earlier composition, size, and few-shot ablations are retained through relocation and merging.

E5.justification: The five-trial bias ablations, 20-random-subset oversight ablation, existing error bars, and pilot correlation/kappa reporting are retained. The new studies introduce no uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing practice. Parenthesized changes in Table 10 are accuracy differences, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds human-audit results of 47 versus 13 mislabeled length-bias samples and 55 versus 33 sycophancy samples for selected versus random subsets. Table 10 adds curated-model accuracies reaching 64.12% on Concise and 71.93% on Less Sycophantic; Table 11 reports AUC 0.620 with HelpSteer2 validation. These are new-setting results; the original headline AUCs of 0.800 and 0.711 and oversight results remain.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 changes the inverse-Hessian approximation prefactor from negative in v1 Equation 6 to positive in v2. Appendix C.2.3 adds missing minus signs to the confidence and entropy formulas. v2 also states a DataInf approximation-error bound in its limitations. The underlying influence-function derivation and assumptions are retained.

C1.justification: The two central applications and computational-efficiency claim remain. The introduction now explicitly extends the demonstrated applicability to naturally mislabeled preference data and claims potential for improving public preference datasets through bias detection and mitigation.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and limitation discussions: approximation error at larger model sizes, restricted dataset/bias coverage, manual validation curation, and distribution mismatch. Appendix G interprets improvements beyond clean-data training as possible correction of pre-existing bias while acknowledging losses on opposing validation subsets. The survey discussion also qualifies judgments through annotator subjectivity.

D1.justification: v2 supplies selection and relabeling recipes and annotation instructions for the added studies. It omits v1's explicit TRL library identification and dedicated statement about supplementary code, dataset links, and replication instructions. The source-code link, primary hyperparameters, hardware, and compression details remain.

R1.justification: Related work expands influence functions' robust-statistics origins and prior image/text applications, adding works such as Rousseeuw and Leroy, Tyler, Cohen et al., and Schioppa et al. New limitations and distribution discussions add further references. The central positioning around DataInf, OPORP, reward modeling, and scalable oversight remains.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main Sections 1–6 sequence are retained. v2 shortens headings and passages, relocates ablation discussions into appendices, makes limitations a standalone section, adds acknowledgments, and revises the author list. These are localized editorial and organizational changes.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, substantially restructuring tables and figure placement. Ablation plots are relocated or merged, and v1's compact qualitative Figure 3 is removed while its examples remain in the appendix. v2 adds survey, retraining, and distribution-comparison tables plus two color-coded original-label example figures.

improvement.justification: v1's bias-detection evidence chiefly concerns injected label errors. v2 addresses this important applicability gap with human audits of original labels and random-sample controls. Retraining experiments demonstrate practical consequences and tradeoffs, while distribution testing and expanded limitations clarify boundaries. Formula corrections also improve correctness. Although uncertainty reporting remains limited and the supplementary reproducibility statement disappears, the new evidence substantially strengthens the central application claims.
